Can you explain to our listeners what caused this collapse and how it is affecting the American people?

Well, thanks, Sarah. I think there's Two causes, there's the proximate cause, the immediate cause, and then there is the underlying cause, which is a little bit, you have to go back in history a little bit to fully understand this story of this bank collapse and similar banks that are in similar distress. So the proximate cause is obviously a lack of strong management by the bank, failure to hedge interest rate risk in a rising interest rate environment. This was an institution that grew very rapidly, quadrupled in size in two years, doubled in size in one year, and took on a whole lot of uninsured deposits. And it was heavily concentrated in the tech and bio sectors. One would expect that coming from Silicon Valley. But over 50% of the market share of all technology startups in the country banked with this one institution, all 50 states. So it was heavily concentrated. And an inordinate amount of uninsured deposits, 90% of the deposits that this bank, this regional bank were uninsured, meaning they had accounts over $250,000 of FDIC insurance. But the main problem with bank management is that they took a very, very risky position, the riskiest investment strategy you could take. They took all of those uninsured deposits and then they invested them in long dated hold to maturity securities, relatively safe securities, by the way, US treasuries and agency securities, mortgage backed securities. But the problem was they invested in those long duration bonds before the Federal Reserve started to tighten monetary policy. And so you had a precipitous increase in interest rates. And there was no hedging of that interest rate risk. And as a result, the value of those assets plummeted. They had unrealized losses. And when the tech sector, which was under duress, began to move money out of the bank. And when there were withdrawals, because the institution marked those assets to market, in the middle of last week and they realized they had all these unrealized losses, well then the bank had to actually sell those assets at a loss in order to cover all of the withdrawals. That caused a bank run that was simply unsustainable and that was what necessitated regulator intervention. But the underlying cause though is the more interesting part of the story, Sarah, because uh... this was a failure not just a bank management this was a failure of government policy it was a failure of bank supervision now you will get some progressives uh... including the president uh... elizabeth warren and others who blame uh... uh... regulatory reform for this but but let's be clear this was not a failure of existing bank regulation The regulators had all the tools that they needed to prevent this from happening. And in fact, over the weekend, when you saw Treasury, the FDIC, and the Fed intervene, they had the tools that they needed to limit the bank run and to address the systemic risk issue over the weekend. This was not a failure of a lack of regulation. This was a failure of bank supervision. And the San Francisco Fed was regulating and supervising this institution, SVB. They were in it. They had all the visibility that they needed. And they failed to address this growing liquidity challenge for this bank. And they failed to identify this interest rate risk that was growing. And it was hiding in plain sight.
